chapterTag.category: AP Calc BC BC-5 — Sequences & Series

body.en: The heart of BC: deciding whether an infinite sum settles to a finite value, using a battery of convergence tests.
Watch the geometric series \( \sum_{n\ge1}\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n} \) converge: each partial sum \( S_N \) climbs toward the limit \( 1 \) (the amber line).

ariaLabel.en: Partial sums of a geometric series approaching their limit

caption.en: Partial sums S(n) up to the current n

note.en: \( S_N=1-\left(\tfrac12\right)^{N}\to1 \); a geometric series converges because \( |r|<1 \).

body.en: nth-term test: if \( a_n\not\to0 \), the series diverges. A geometric series converges when \( |r|<1 \); a p-series when \( p>1 \). The comparison, ratio, and alternating series tests handle the rest.

figure.title: Convergence of Geometric Partial Sums: S_N = 1 - (1/2)^N

caption.en: Partial sums $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N (1/2)^n = 1 - (1/2)^N$ climb monotonically toward the horizontal asymptote $S = 1$. Because $|r| = 1/2 < 1$, the infinite series converges to $\frac{a}{1-r} = \frac{1/2}{1 - 1/2} = 1$.

label.en: ⚠️ AP Exam Traps: Infinite Series Convergence Tests

body.en:
• The \( n \)-th Term Divergence Test Never Proves Convergence: If \( \lim a_n \neq 0 \), the series diverges. However, if \( \lim a_n = 0 \), the test is INCONCLUSIVE! The harmonic series \( \sum \frac{1}{n} \) has terms approaching \( 0 \), but it diverges. Never write 'converges by the \( n \)-th term test' on an AP exam.
  • Ratio Test Inconclusiveness: If \( \lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| = 1 \), the Ratio Test fails completely. The Ratio Test cannot determine the convergence of \( p \)-series or algebraic fractions (it always gives \( 1 \)). Use the Limit Comparison Test with a \( p \)-series instead.
  • Alternating Series Test (AST) Hypotheses: To earn full credit for AST on an FRQ, you must explicitly state that (1) terms alternate in sign, (2) terms decrease in magnitude (\( |a_{n+1}| \le |a_n| \)), and (3) \( \lim_{n\to\infty} |a_n| = 0 \).
  • Alternating Error Bound: If an alternating series converges by AST, the truncation error when using the \( N \)-th partial sum \( S_N \) is bounded by the magnitude of the first omitted term: \( |S - S_N| \le |a_{N+1}| \).

Determine whether \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\dfrac{n!}{n^n}\) converges.\[L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{(n+1)!/(n+1)^{n+1}}{n!/n^n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^n}{(n+1)^n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n=\frac{1}{e}<1.\]

Ratio test: \(L<1\), so the series converges.

question.en: Find the interval of convergence of \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\dfrac{(-1)^n x^n}{n}\).

solution.en: Ratio test: \(|x|\). Converges absolutely for \(|x|<1\). At \(x=1\): alternating harmonic series, converges. At \(x=-1\): harmonic series, diverges. Interval of convergence: \(-1<x\leq1\).

question.en: Determine whether the series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}\) converges absolutely, converges conditionally, or diverges.

solution.en: First test absolute convergence: \(\sum\left|\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}\right| = \sum\frac{1}{n^{1/2}}\). This is a \(p\)-series with \(p = 1/2 \le 1\), which diverges. Next test the original alternating series using AST: the terms alternate in sign, \(b_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\) is strictly decreasing (\(b_{n+1} < b_n\)), and \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} = 0\). By the Alternating Series Test, the series converges. Since the series converges but does not converge absolutely, it converges conditionally.
